aiOverview.content: Yes, Virginia experiences earthquakes, though they are usually small (magnitude 2–4) and infrequent. While not in a high-risk tectonic boundary zone, Virginia has three main seismic zones—most notably in Central Virginia and Giles County. Damaging earthquakes can occur, such as the 2011 magnitude 5.8 Mineral, VA earthquake that was felt throughout the East Coast. Key Seismic Areas in Virginia: Central Virginia Seismic Zone (CVSZ): Centered near Richmond, this zone causes frequent minor shakes. Giles County Seismic Zone (GCSZ): Located along the New River Valley, this is a very active zone. Eastern Tennessee Seismic Zone (ETSZ): Affects far southwestern Virginia. Key Facts on Virginia Earthquakes: Rarity vs. Strength: Small earthquakes are fairly common, while strong earthquakes are rare. Location: Earthquakes often occur along ancient, inactive-looking faults. Historical Quakes: The largest in Virginia was a 5.8 magnitude in 1897 and the 2011 Mineral event. Impact: Because Virginia is in the interior of the North American plate, earthquakes can be felt over a broader area than on the West Coast. For information on how to prepare for seismic activity, residents can visit the VDEM Earthquakes and Landslides page. VDEM Earthquakes and Landslides
